aulas.objetivo: Fazer um simulado com os formatos da prova C1 Advanced: leitura longa, cloze, word formation e key word transformation.
aulas.foco: Mock exam: Parts 1-5 of CAE Reading and Use of English
explicacao: Este simulado reúne os formatos de Reading & Use of English: Part 1 (multiple-choice cloze), Part 2 (open cloze), Part 3 (word formation), Part 4 (key word transformation) e Part 5 (texto longo com atitude do autor).
Leia o texto uma vez para a ideia geral, depois volte para cada pergunta. Em Part 5, elimine as opções que repetem palavras do texto mas mudam o sentido.
Em Part 4, mantenha a palavra-chave sem mudar e use de 3 a 5 palavras. Confira tempos verbais e preposições.
Gerencie o tempo: no exame real, são 90 minutos para as 8 partes. Aqui, respire e responda com calma.

material.texto:
When I began translating novels twenty-five years ago, I assumed that the profession would one day be quietly retired by technology. I did not imagine that the retirement would be announced by software that could translate a paragraph in a fraction of a second, and could do so, disconcertingly, rather well. The first time I fed one of my own translations into such a program and compared the results, I felt something between professional alarm and unexpected curiosity. The machine had produced a competent version. It had also, in a sentence I had spent an hour on, produced a mistake so confident that I laughed aloud.

It is tempting to describe the difference as one of accuracy, but that would be to misunderstand the task. A literary translator is not only converting words; she is deciding which of the author's habits to preserve and which to sacrifice. A writer who repeats a word obsessively may be establishing a rhythm, or may simply lack an editor, and the translator has to judge which. Software, by contrast, tends to smooth out oddities, producing text that is fluent but strangely flat. The result reads like a good imitation of a book, rather than a book.

None of this prevents publishers from taking an interest. Margins in the industry are thin, translated fiction accounts for a small share of sales in English-speaking countries, and the temptation to cut costs is obvious. Several colleagues have already been offered contracts in which they are asked simply to 'edit' a machine draft, at a fraction of their usual rate. I have declined two such offers, not out of pride but because correcting a draft often takes longer than starting again. One has to unlearn the machine's mistakes before one can see the author's meaning, and it is hard to do both at once.

Still, I would be dishonest if I claimed to be unaffected. I now find myself using the software for the least interesting work: the first pass through a technical manual, say, or a tedious letter. It saves time, and I cannot pretend that I miss the typing. The danger, as I see it, is subtle. If translators come to treat the machine's version as a starting point, there is a risk that its choices will become the default, and over time a kind of average style will creep into every book we read. The variety that makes literature worth translating in the first place would, ironically, be the first casualty.

My younger colleagues are more optimistic than I am, and perhaps they are right. They point out that photography did not destroy painting, though it changed what painters were for. I find this argument comforting rather than convincing. Painting survived because people discovered that they cared about something a camera could not give them. Whether readers will care, in sufficient numbers, about the invisible labour of a translator is a question to which I have no answer. What I do know is that on the day the machine learns to laugh at its own mistakes, I shall begin to worry.

exercicios.q: What was the writer's reaction when she first compared the machine's version with her own?
op: She decided at once to stop translating.
She was relieved that it was so inaccurate.
She was horrified by how good it was.
She felt a mixture of concern and interest, and amusement at one error.
exercicios.exp: 'something between professional alarm and unexpected curiosity' e 'I laughed aloud' diante do erro. Part 5.

exercicios.q: What does the writer mean by saying the translator must decide 'which of the author's habits to preserve'?
op: Every habit must be copied exactly.
Authors should work with editors more.
Translators should correct an author's faults.
Some repetition may be deliberate, so judgement is needed.
exercicios.exp: 'may be establishing a rhythm, or may simply lack an editor, and the translator has to judge which'. A questão é julgamento, não cópia nem correção automática. Part 5.

exercicios.q: Software tends to smooth out oddities, producing text that is fluent but strangely ___. (EXPRESS)
exercicios.exp: Adjetivo negativo a partir de express: inexpressive (sem expressão). 'Flat' no texto expressa o mesmo sentido. Part 3.

exercicios.q: Leia em voz alta.
exercicios.frase: On the day the machine learns to laugh at its own mistakes, I shall begin to worry.
exercicios.exp: Pausa depois de 'mistakes'. 'Shall' é formal e britânico: /ʃæl/ ou /ʃəl/.

exercicios.q: Why has the writer refused to 'edit' machine drafts?
op: The rates are too low for her pride.
Publishers have not made any offers.
She dislikes using computers.
Correcting often takes longer than translating from scratch.
exercicios.exp: 'not out of pride but because correcting a draft often takes longer than starting again'. A resposta está explícita; a opção do orgulho é negada. Part 5.

exercicios.q: Margins in the industry are thin, ___ the temptation to cut costs is obvious. (one word)
exercicios.exp: Open cloze (Part 2): conector de consequência. Margens pequenas, por isso a tentação de cortar custos. Aceitamos so ou hence.

exercicios.q:
'I haven't finished the translation yet,' she said. STILL
She said that she ___ the translation.
exercicios.exp: Discurso indireto com STILL: still hadn't finished / had still not finished. Part 4.

exercicios.q: Choose the word that best fits: Several colleagues have been offered contracts at a ___ of their usual rate.
op: division
fraction
segment
portion
exercicios.exp: Collocation: at a fraction of the rate/price = por uma pequena parte do valor. Part 1 (multiple-choice cloze).

exercicios.q:
The writer fears that over time a kind of average style will creep into every book. DANGER
There is ___ an average style will creep into every book.
exercicios.exp: Com DANGER: there is a danger that + oração. Part 4.

exercicios.q: Responda em inglês: você acha que a tecnologia pode substituir tradutores ou artistas? Dê sua opinião com um exemplo.
exercicios.frase: Do you think technology will replace translators or artists?
exercicios.modelo: Personally, I do not believe it will replace them completely. Although machines can imitate a style, they lack human judgement, whereas translators understand the culture behind the words.
exercicios.exp: Use conectores da aula 10: whereas, although, provided that, albeit.

exercicios.q: What is the writer's attitude to her younger colleagues' comparison with photography and painting?
op: She is entirely persuaded by it.
She finds it reassuring but is not truly convinced.
She thinks it is unrelated to translation.
She believes it is offensive.
exercicios.exp: 'comforting rather than convincing' = reconfortante, mas não convincente. Part 5.

exercicios.q:
The machine can't distinguish between a deliberate repetition and a careless one. ABLE
The machine ___ a deliberate repetition from a careless one.
exercicios.exp: Com ABLE: is not able to + verbo (tell ... from / distinguish ... from). Part 4.
